articles.text: After an 11-month absence due to the COVID pandemic, Piedmont’s three elementary schools welcomed new friends on Tuesday, February 9. Kindergarteners, the youngest scholars in town, were the first to return to in-person learning aside from a class of nine TK students at Beach, a handful of SPED learners and a portion of students at Millennium High. Today, Wednesday, 1st graders that have selected the in-person/ hybrid model will return to class, and on Thursday 2nd graders will be added. TK-2 will continue on Friday, before the one-week Ski Week break February 15-19. The district plans to use that week to make any adjustments needed after this week of in-person education. On February 23, the Tuesday following the weeklong break, students in 3rd and 6th grades will return to their campuses. On February 24 schools will add 4th graders, and by February 25, fifth graders will return to complete the phased-in reopening of schools. Classes are divided into two cohorts, morning and afternoon, to allow for classes to have 15 or fewer students. In-person school days will be 2 hours and 15 minutes from Tuesday through Friday. articles.text: No new cases reported in Piedmont in a week No new cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont in the past seven days, representing a significant slowdown in new cases after a terrible winter surge rocked Piedmont, Alameda County and California. As of Monday, February 8, there have been 162 reported cases in the City in the past 11 months. Coronavirus continues to spread through the county, though. The number of daily new cases and the positivity rate are both significantly higher than in September and October of last year. Across Alameda County, 2,448 new cases have been reported across the past seven days, which represents about a 27 percent decrease in new cases week-over-week. The total caseload for the county is 77,109. There have been 23,940 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,129 cases in Hayward. Tragically, 60 more people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County across the past seven days, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,051. Even though stricter stay-athome orders were lifted a few weeks ago, Alameda County remains in the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric for reopening economic activity. Only five counties in California – none of which are in the Bay Area – are not in the Purple Tier. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 4 percent, more than a full percentage point lower than one week ago. While the positivity rate is low enough that Alameda County could move into a less restrictive tier for reopening businesses and activities, the adjusted cases per day per 100,000 people in the county is 18.1. This figure needs to be below 7 for the county to reopen further, according to California’s current system. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,354,591 total cases of COVID- 19 in California, making it the hardest hit state by the virus by far. There have been 44,477 deaths due to the disease statewide.

articles.text: Earlier this month Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a second reading of local energy efficiency ordinances, also called reach codes (Ordinances 750 and 751 N.S.). Reach codes are local building energy codes that reach beyond statewide requirements for energy use in building design and construction. Piedmont is one of the first cities nationwide to tie reach codes to renovations of existing residential buildings. This is a landmark achievement for local climate action. It also reflects steps toward meeting the community standards outlined in Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan (CAP) 2.0. Reach codes address objectives set forth by the CAP 2.0, including increasing the use of solar energy systems and reducing natural gas use in residential buildings. Building energy is a primary cause of emissions in the City, comprising roughly half of Piedmont’s community emissions in 2018. Building energy in 2018 resulted in approximately 16,892 metric tons of CO2e, with most emissions coming from natural gas furnaces and water heaters. Measures such as the reach codes position the City to meet CAP 2.0 emissions reduction goals: reduce emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030 and 80% below 2005 levels by 2050. The ordinances are intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and achieve energy savings. They will also improve indoor air quality and health. Momentum continues to build towards enacting electrification reach codes. In addition to Piedmont, more than 40 cities and counties in California are considering or adopting local reach codes, with various approaches and requirements. This includes the nearby cities of Oakland, Berkeley, Albany, Alameda, Hayward, Fremont, Richmond, and San Francisco. Individually, these municipalities are designing pathways to reduce natural gas use and taking into account local sociocultural, political, and economic needs. Collectively, these efforts work towards achieving local and statewide climate action and energy goals. As Piedmont moves forward with the reach code approval process, including submission to the California Energy Commission and California Building Standards Commission, the City staff is preparing frameworks and resources geared at homeowners, contractors, and planners alike. These materials are forthcoming and will be posted on the City’s website. The City staff will also look to share best practices and lessons learned from the reach codes process. In turn, it is hoped that Piedmont’s reach codes will serve as a model for other municipalities that are considering the adoption of energy efficiency requirements. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be contacted at (510)420-3058 or adykman@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Oakland Coliseum vaccination site to open next week People age 65 years and older, in addition to emergency services workers and essential education workers are among a new group of people that began receiving COVID-19 vaccines in Alameda County this week on Monday, February 8. The county first announced the change on Wednesday, February 3, saying that it would begin vaccinating people in Phase 1B Tier 1 as defined by the state’s vaccination framework. Phase 1B Tier 1 includes people age 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. This entire group of people numbers approximately 325,000 residents according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Concurrently, people in Phase 1A continue to be vaccinated. This group includes healthcare workers and residents and staff of long-term care facilities. They were the first to be eligible when the first doses of vaccine arrived in December. In Alameda County, Phase 1A includes an estimated 145,000 people. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider or employer to receive a vaccination appointment. “We’ve made great progress on vaccinating health care workers in Phase 1A and are happy to be moving forward with Phase 1B,” wrote Dr. Kathleen Clanon, the county’s lead on vaccine planning. “Our strategy is to reach people who are at highest risk for severe illness and people who are at high risk for transmission because of where they live or work.” Alameda County waited a few weeks and continued to focus on Phase 1A before opening up eligibility to Phase 1B Tier 1. The state allowed counties to begin vaccinating the latter phase on January 26. Next week on Tuesday, February 16, the Oakland Coliseum is expected to open as a large vaccination site. Announced last week, the project is a partnership between the state and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). “This additional resource and infusion of vaccine is much needed in our community and will help us to reach more people more quickly,” said Colleen Chawla, director of the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency (HCSA). “We look forward to working with the site team to support outreach, education and access for our highest risk communities.” Gov. Gavin Newsom praised Alameda County’s vaccination efforts last week. “One county stands out in terms of their speed to administration, taking vaccines and getting people vaccinated, and that’s Alameda County,” Newsom said, adding, “I want to just recognize their partnership, their stewardship to the cause.” Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. pages.text: Wednesday, February 10, 2021 3 News COVID NEWS Alameda County COVID-19 positivity rate dips to 4 percent No new cases reported in Piedmont in a week By Barry Eitel No new cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont in the past seven days, representing a significant slowdown in new cases after a terrible winter surge rocked Piedmont, Alameda County and California. As of Monday, February 8, there have been 162 reported cases in the City in the past 11 months. Coronavirus continues to spread through the county, though. The number of daily new cases and the positivity rate are both significantly higher than in September and October of last year. Across Alameda County, 2,448 new cases have been reported across the past seven days, which represents about a 27 percent decrease in new cases week-over-week. The total caseload for the county is 77,109. There have been 23,940 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,129 cases in Hayward. Tragically, 60 more people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County across the past seven days, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,051. Even though stricter stay-athome orders were lifted a few weeks ago, Alameda County remains in the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric for reopening economic activity. Only five counties in California – none of which are in the Bay Area – are not in the Purple Tier. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 4 percent, more than a full percentage point lower than one week ago. While the positivity rate is low enough that Alameda County could move into a less restrictive tier for reopening businesses and activities, the adjusted cases per day per 100,000 people in the county is 18.1. This figure needs to be below 7 for the county to reopen further, according to California’s current system. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,354,591 total cases of COVID- 19 in California, making it the hardest hit state by the virus by far. There have been 44,477 deaths due to the disease statewide. Vaccination for seniors begins in Alameda County Oakland Coliseum vaccination site to open next week By Barry Eitel People age 65 years and older, in addition to emergency services workers and essential education workers are among a new group of people that began receiving COVID-19 vaccines in Alameda County this week on Monday, February 8. The county first announced the change on Wednesday, February 3, saying that it would begin vaccinating people in Phase 1B Tier 1 as defined by the state’s vaccination framework. Phase 1B Tier 1 includes people age 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. This entire group of people numbers approximately 325,000 residents according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Concurrently, people in Phase 1A continue to be vaccinated. This group includes healthcare workers and residents and staff of long-term care facilities. They were the first to be eligible when the first doses of vaccine arrived in December. In Alameda County, Phase 1A includes an estimated 145,000 people. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider or employer to receive a vaccination appointment. “We’ve made great progress on vaccinating health care workers in Phase 1A and are happy to be moving forward with Phase 1B,” wrote Dr. Kathleen Clanon, the county’s lead on vaccine planning. “Our strategy is to reach people who are at highest risk for severe illness and people who are at high risk for transmission because of where they live or work.” Alameda County waited a few weeks and continued to focus on Phase 1A before opening up eligibility to Phase 1B Tier 1. The state allowed counties to begin vaccinating the latter phase on January 26. Next week on Tuesday, February 16, the Oakland Coliseum is expected to open as a large vaccination site. Announced last week, the project is a partnership between the state and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). “This additional resource and infusion of vaccine is much needed in our community and will help us to reach more people more quickly,” said Colleen Chawla, director of the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency (HCSA). “We look forward to working with the site team to support outreach, education and access for our highest risk communities.” Gov. Gavin Newsom praised Alameda County’s vaccination efforts last week. “One county stands out in terms of their speed to administration, taking vaccines and getting people vaccinated, and that’s Alameda County,” Newsom said, adding, “I want to just recognize their partnership, their stewardship to the cause.” See Vaccination on page 30 Reach Codes landmark: Local Climate Action initiatives approved By Alyssa Dykman Earlier this month Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a second reading of local energy efficiency ordinances, also called reach codes (Ordinances 750 and 751 N.S.). Reach codes are local building energy codes that reach beyond statewide requirements for energy use in building design and construction. Piedmont is one of the first cities nationwide to tie reach codes to renovations of existing residential buildings. This is a landmark achievement for local climate action. It also reflects steps toward meeting the community standards outlined in Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan (CAP) 2.0. Reach codes address objectives set forth by the CAP 2.0, including increasing the use of solar energy systems and reducing natural gas use in residential buildings. Building energy is a primary cause of emissions in the City, comprising roughly half of Piedmont’s community emissions in 2018. Building energy in 2018 resulted in approximately 16,892 metric tons of CO2e, with most emissions coming from natural gas furnaces and water heaters. Measures such as the reach codes position the City to meet CAP 2.0 emissions reduction goals: reduce emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030 and 80% below 2005 levels by 2050. The ordinances are intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and achieve energy savings. They will also improve indoor air quality and health. Momentum continues to build towards enacting electrification reach codes. In addition to Piedmont, more than 40 cities and counties in California are considering or adopting local reach codes, with various approaches and requirements. This includes the nearby cities of Oakland, Berkeley, Albany, Alameda, Hayward, Fremont, Richmond, and San Francisco. Individually, these municipalities are designing pathways to reduce natural gas use and taking into account local sociocultural, political, and economic needs. Collectively, these efforts work towards achieving local and statewide climate action and energy goals. As Piedmont moves forward with the reach code approval process, including submission to the California Energy Commission and California Building Standards Commission, the City staff is preparing frameworks and resources geared at homeowners, contractors, and planners alike. These materials are forthcoming and will be posted on the City’s website. The City staff will also look to share best practices and lessons learned from the reach codes process. In turn, it is hoped that Piedmont’s reach codes will serve as a model for other municipalities that are considering the adoption of energy efficiency requirements. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be contacted at (510)420-3058 or adykman@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will hold a public forum on homelessness on March 2. articles.text: Fireworks and family feasts At Chinese New Year celebrations people wear red clothes, decorate with poems on red paper, and give children and single people “crisp lucky money” in red envelopes or “hong bao.” Red symbolizes fire and good luck, which according to legend can drive away bad luck. The fireworks that shower the festivities also drive away evil spirits. Tangerines and oranges represent prosperity. On New Year, families clean their houses, wear new clothes, visit each other, get together for dinner and exchange food gifts. Due to COVID-19, there will be no Chinese New Year parade this year, but the Chinese Chamber of Commerce of San Francisco has commissioned several parade float artists to celebrate the Year of the Ox with 11 lifesized ox statues that now stand tall and proud at various locations across the city. One is even at the Oakland airport, and another at the San Francisco airport. There is one in Chinatown at Portsmouth Square and another at the Chinese Hospital. Gung Hay Fat Choy (Gong Xi Fa Cai) – “May you be happy and prosperous.” Lunar New Year is the longest and most important celebration in Asia, with over 1.5 billion people across the globe celebrating the new year in China, Vietnam, Korea, and Singapore for two weeks. Even during the Vietnam war, the Lunar New Year, a holiday called Tet, North and South Vietnamese forces would traditionally call a truce to allow soldiers to return to their families to celebrate. The Chinese year 4719, Year of the Ox, begins on Feb. 12, 2021. The Chinese use the lunar calendar, which has 13 months which explains why Lunar New Year changes every year. times, Buddha asked all the animals to meet him on Chinese New Happy Ox hunting! Year. But only 12 animals came. In order to decide their order in the Chinese Zodiac cycle, the animals held a very exciting race. The first one to cross the river to the finish line would be granted the first year, the second to come in would be the second animal in the cycle, and so on. The strong, hardworking Ox was in the lead with the Rat close by. Suddenly, the clever Rat asked the good-natured Ox for a ride on its back, but then at the last second before reaching shore, the ungrateful Rat jumped off on land to cross the finish line first to win the race. The Ox came in second, the Tiger third, and so on. The happy-go-lucky Pig took his time and came in last, and the Chinese Zodiac and its twelve signs were born... Buddha named a year after each animal and the cycle would repeat every 12 years. He announced that the people born in each animal’s year would have some of that animal’s personality. People under the Year of the Ox are usually hard working, honest, creative, ambitious, cautious, patient and handle things steadily. On the negative side, Ox people might be stubborn, narrow-minded, indifferent, prejudiced, slow and not good at communication. The Ox is a highly esteemed animal in Chinese culture because of the important role it plays in agriculture. Positive traits, such as hardworking and honest, are also attributed to the Ox. Their dedication and diligence make them ideal for professional and stressful positions such as doctors, lawyers, businessmen, politicians and teachers. Oxen are also renowned by society for their technical skills and effort in computer and engineering. Famous people like Barack Obama, Walt Disney, Princess Diana and George Clooney were born under the year of the ox. If you are an ox, this year you will be either age 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, or older. Oranges and tangerines are symbols of prosperity. Red envelopes and lucky money (hong bao).

articles.text: Marin County has had nearly all its public schools open since early last fall. They began opening up elementary and middle schools as early as September 8. With 18 school districts, almost 40,000 students and 7,000 staff, the county has had only 10 suspected in-school COVID-19 transmissions. They owe their success to a healthy relationship with a cooperative Marin County Public Health Department and lower COVID case counts than Alameda County. mont and other local school districts were still talking about possibly reopening classes, the Marin County district had logged a cumulative 800,000 student days. As of February 8, they had only 15 individual schools doing remote only learning. In the meantime, 101 schools (87 percent) were open with at least 10 percent of students in-person. Within the entire county there have been a total of 164 COVID- 19 positive cases for students, and 42 among staff. But only 10 transmissions are suspected to have occurred in school in the five months since last fall. To view their transmission and school data go to coronavirus. marinhhs.org/schools#status. “The true heroes in this are the teachers, classified staff and administration who have worked tirelessly with Public Health to bring our students back in-person,” said Marin County’s Superintendent Mary Jane Burke. While they don’t currently have high schools open, they have created in-person “Learning Hubs” for high schoolers. Hub sites are on campuses or at community centers like the YMCA, where students can do all their distance learning. The learning hubs provide a safe space, supportive adult supervision, social interaction with peers, and broadband internet access. Marin’s first Learning Hub opened at the same time as its elementary and middle schools, September 8. By December 29, 55 hubs were open in Marin County, serving 1,750 students. The Deputy Superintendent of the Marin County Office of Education, Terena Mares, described the advantage Marin County has over Alameda County: a healthy, pre-existing relationship with their Public Health Department. “We worked really closely and extensively with our County Public Health Department, and they were hugely instrumental in assisting us to create the safe kind of environments that they could put their seal on,” Mares said. “We have worked closely in the past with them on issues related to air quality and measles vaccination.” “Our public health officers have just been very approachable to work to ensure that when we open, we open safely in a way that recognizes that students are actually safer in person than they are while at home. The data is proving that,” Mares added. Those following the efforts to reopen schools in Alameda County have seen a far different story. In June, Alameda County’s Public Health Officer, Erica Pan, was promoted to the state level, thrusting Interim Officer Nicolas Moss into leadership during the greatest public health crisis in decades. Communication has not been clear between Alameda County’s public health office and schools. UCSF Professor of Epidemiology and Piedmont resident Dr. George Rutherford commented on another difference between the conditions in Marin County and Alameda County. “Marin has done a better job than others at keeping their most vulnerable [blue collar, multi-generation household] populations

articles.text: Brooke Hendershott of Piedmont, was named to the College of the Holy Cross Dean’s List for the Fall semester. A sophomore, Hendershott is majoring in Chemistry. A total of 1,453 students were named to the Dean’s List for outstanding academic achievement. To qualify, students must pass four or more letter-graded courses with no failing grades during the semester and earn a GPA of 3.5 or higher. articles.text: We tend to think of attention as something simple. We are paying attention, or we are not. Actually, attention is a complex cognitive function which, like other multifaceted cognitive functions, matures throughout childhood. Inattention is undesirable, as is too much attention. But is distractibility a feature of attention, or a glitch? The goal is: efficient, flexible and voluntary control of our attentional resources. Nuanced attention is the basis for planning, organization, self-control and perseverance. Neuroscientists have identified the part of the brain that is important in being able to attend to one stimulus and ignore others (known as selective attention) as the prefrontal cortex. Maturation of the nervous system allows for changing from global to selective attention. Infants as young as 4 months of age attend to differences in their environment. At around 10 months of age infants can show signs of resistance to distractions. play focused attention, and by age 3, around the time many children enter preschool, their attention to task is increasing. Studies show that attention is somewhat malleable. For example, children in preschool and elementary school show decreased attention to distractors when given frequent instructions to do so. Parents and teachers can scaffold their instructions accordingly to increase the student’s attention and decrease attention to a distracting event. Children show decreased attention when experiencing distress or negative emotionality. Parents and teachers can focus on praise and warm, positive emotional environments which may correlate with improved attention. Why is selective attention critical for classroom success? Estimates are as much as 80% of classroom education is with a teacher talking and students attending, so selective attention is key. The classroom requires selective and sustained attention to a specific target (the teacher, or written materials) with the simultaneous ability to ignore distractions. One of the most common teacher/parent concerns is that their student is having trouble paying attention. The student may be “tuning out”, easily distracted, impulsive and looking around to see what everyone else is doing because he/she cannot sustain attention to the teacher. On the other hand, school activities such as art, P.E and team sports require less selective attention. In these classes more global attention is required, to pay attention to many details, sights and sounds simultaneously. When kids enter the formal school system, they are moving from the global attention of multi-sensory experiences such as play, sports and media to the selective attention of sitting still and selectively listening to a teacher. In the case of school-aged kids who are struggling with attention in the classroom, physiological issues to consider may be poor sleep, blood sugar imbalances, or vision or hearing issues. Psychological issues to consider may be anxiety, decreased confidence or perfectionism. Learning issues to consider may be sensory or auditory processing difficulties. Depending on the etiology of the observed attentional difficulties, treatment can include medication, parent training in behavior management, classroom interventions, as well as therapy. articles.text: Part of Readmont 2021, the annual community read A panel discussion titled “Embracing Clean Energy” will be held on February 25 from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m. as the first of three panel discussions as part of Readmont, the annual community read in Piedmont. This year’s selection is Naomi Klein’s book This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate. The panelists include: • Jessica Tovar of the Local Clean Energy Alliance in Oakland, an NGO working in advocacy for clean energy. (http:// localcleanenergy.org/) • Angel Fierro, husband of Millennium HS principal Shannon Fierro and co-partner of Plexus Solutions, which joins large scale clean energy projects with capital. http://www.plexussolutions.services/leadership • Dr. Max Auffhammer, George Pardee Jr. Professor of Sustainable Development and Associate Dean in the Division of Social Sciences at UC Berkeley. He is also an Assistant Professor of Agricultural and Resource Economics and International and Area Studies at UC Berkeley and Chair at the Political Economy, UC Berkeley. (https://onpointanalytics.com/ experts/maximilian-auffhammer/) This year, Readmont teamed up with Piedmont Connect to host book discussions at Piedmont High School. To register, visit piedmontconnect.org/readmont-2021. The hope is that this common reading experience will forge positive connections among students, staff, parents and community members. The next event will be “Youth Summit on Environmental Justice” on April 24, an event open to high school students across the Bay Area, ready to take action to preserve the planet. All Piedmonters are encouraged to read This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate by Naomi Klein. The author argues that climate change should not be put on a shelf and studied, but is a problem that requires fixing the economic system that she sees as already in trouble. Copies are available for checkout at the PHS library. Interested readers can contact PHS Librarian Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@ piedmont.k12.ca.us to borrow a copy. articles.text: Piedmont Scout Council, BSA has announced a year-long celebration with a virtual auction, an opportunity to honor someone special, and the annual recognition dinner the week of March 17-25. The campaign will celebrate the centennial year of the Piedmont Scout Council as a chartered organization with the Boy Scouts of America. Titled “You Raise Me Up”, the campaign aims to raise awareness of Piedmont Scouts and their contributions to the community over 100 years. Chartered on March 21, 1921, the Piedmont Scout Council is one of the largest youth development organizations in the city. Its focus is character-building and teaching important life skills in leadership, citizenship, scholarship, sportsmanship and outdoorsmanship. Piedmont Scouts have evolved through the years and support the pursuits of over 1,000 boys and girls, ages 5-17 across a variety of programs, including Cub Scouts, Scouts, Explorers, Venturers and Piedmont Language School. The “Raise Me Up” campaign launches on March 17 with a virtual auction and will culminate on March 25 with a virtual version of the annual recognition dinner for community volunteers. The entire community is invited to participate in the auction and to honor their favorite Scout, Scout leader or someone important with an engraved anniversary brick. Each brick will be $100 and enshrined in a manner to be announced. Registration is free and open to the community. The auction will offer a variety of items, including vacations at beautiful vacation homes, food and wine, and themed gift baskets. Access to the auction, anniversary commemorative bricks, and recognition dinner is available at www.piedmontbsa.org. To learn more contact Kate Benson at the Scout Council office, tel. 547-4493 or by e-mail at Katherine.benson@scouting.org. Visit the Scout Council also on www.piedmontbsa.org, Facebook (www. facebook.com/PiedmontBSA) and Instagram (PiedmontBSA). History of Piedmont Scouting Piedmont Scouts have proudly served the community since 1910 when the first troop overnight event was held in Redwood Canyon in Oakland. The council was chartered eleven years later, in 1921, by the National Boy Scouts of America. Although it is one of the oldest and smallest councils in the nation, it is widely recognized for its excellence and traditions of service and quality programs. Year after year more than 50% of the eligible youth in Piedmont participate in the council’s many programs, with more than 1000 boys and girls. In support of these youth are 300 adult volunteers and three full-time staff members.

articles.text: Tourists from outside the continent are missing in action on the Paris scene and have been since early last March. If only the City we know had not gone missing with them. Anyone can have a look at the Eiffel Tower, but the thrill of riding to the top isn’t an option. Parks are open, though the winter weather isn’t terribly cooperative and stingy with brief spots of sun. Sacré-Coeur, the Basilica of the Sacred Heart is open daily in Montmartre; but Notre Dame Cathedral remains closed since the fire almost two years ago, and construction work is stalled. The Champs-Elysées is open for strolling the shops, but no cafés, bars or eateries. The grands magasins, department stores Galleries Lafayette and B.H.V., a stone’s throw from our apartment, just closed again due to viral resurgence. On the Left Bank, Boulevard Saint-Germain offers an almost two-mile stretch of fascinating stores, most of them open, but here, too, the museums – d’Orsay, Rodin (except its sculpture garden), Musée of the Moyen Âge (Cluny) remain closed. Cross-country and girls tennis are fall sports. But this year they will be competing in the spring, combining their seasons with track & field and boys’ tennis. Due to massive rescheduling caused by the coronavirus pandemic and the high school having been closed for 11 months, everyone wants to make the new gerrymandered schedule work. “We’re just happy to have tennis back,” said tennis coach Jim Landes. Out of necessity, he will be coaching the girls’ team and boys’ team concurrently, squeezing in enough matches for each team to have a relatively full season. “It’s not a season for the record books this year. We’re there to have fun. It will look different, but we’re happy to have competition again. It’s a season we’ll be playing by ear,’ he added. Later this month, the coed cross-country and track & field teams will toe the line for the school’s first official athletic competition since boys’ lacrosse closed out March 2020. On February 27, the Western Alameda County Conference will hold a virtually timed twomile event, officially the first cross-country meet of the season. The event is the first of just four for cross-country, which will likely occur at the Witter Field track. However, the league is still scrambling to finalize official locations for each of the four cross-country events. “We have meet dates, but we aren’t sure how the meets are going to transpire yet,” said PHS cross-country and track coach Jeanine Holmlund. “Some events for cross-country are up in the air because the issue is where can we run?” Piedmont’s running programs will both compete in the Foothill Division against Bishop O’Dowd, Alameda, Berkeley, San Leandro, Castro Valley, and possibly Hayward. But instead of the usual meets with three or four schools, the league will focus strictly on dual meets between two schools. Cross-country dates are on Saturdays, Feb. 27, March 13, March 27, a possible league championship on April 10, and possible makeup dates from April 12-17. Track, meanwhile, has seven possible meets, including a league championship. articles.text: Bill and Mary Geong pose for a photo during a cruise while celebrating their 42nd wedding anniversary. Bill and Mary Geong plan on having a casual Valentine’s Day at home this year, with one caveat: Mary will not be cooking dinner. Instead, they will be ordering in from her favorite restaurant, Commis, and reflect on their 45 years together. The couple’s history goes back farther than 1976, though; they actually first met in high school in San Francisco. They were in the same homeroom, but didn’t really get to know each other until after graduation. At the time, Mary worked a part-time job in the Tenderloin district. Bill, she said, would routinely offer to walk her to work whenever they found each other riding the same city bus. “He was always offering to walk me to work, and he called me a lot… I thought, this guy must really like me!” Mary said with a smile. They dated for about a year in college, and then decided to “part ways,” and Mary took a one-year teaching job in New Jersey. The calls from Bill didn’t stop, though; one day he called her when she was on the East Coast and she told him that she was ready to return to California, noting that the change of seasons on the East Coast was not for her. “I experienced it for one year, but I wanted to come home after my one-year contract was up. I was homesick, I guess I just wasn’t accustomed to the cold. He asked me when I would be arriving, and that he would pick me up from the airport,” she recalled. “I thought, why not? Someone can help me with my luggage.” Years later, the couple got engaged and then married in 1976. They moved from San Francisco to Oakland, and then eventually moved to Piedmont in search of a competent school district for their growing family. Their daughters, Jennifer and Danielle, both attended Piedmont schools. Jennifer and her husband live in Belarus, and Danielle and husband live in Washington D.C. Bill and Mary are able to keep in touch thanks to our now omni-digital landscape. Asked if Valentine’s Day is significant for the couple, Mary said that she and Bill are very traditional in their celebrations. Dinner reservations at a nice restaurant in town are the norm. The pandemic will weather those plans just a bit, but they still plan on ordering from Commis, a two-star Michelin restaurant on Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. “And every Valentine’s Day, I remind my husband to get me some flowers,” Mary said with a chuckle. Valentine’s Day is actually secondary to the couple this year. A holiday with much more significance is Lunar New Year, which is roughly a week after Valentine’s Day. Mary was born during the Year of the Ox, the animal within the Chinese Zodiac that is observed this New Year. Lunar New Year begins on February 12, just two days before Valentine’s Day, and culminates with festivities on February 20. Mary confessed that she will be busy preparing celebratory activities for her colleagues at Oakland Rotary Club. The Geongs’ relationship with the holiday, like their marriage, goes back many years: Mary is a member of the Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC), a group that was founded in the late 1980s. She has served on its board for more than 20 years and was its former president. During her time on the board, PAAC expanded its membership to include a more diverse group of Asians, to include students from Burmese, Indian, Filipino and Korean cultures. It is one of the longest-standing organizations in the city. In addition to organizing upcoming virtual events, as a Certified Public Accountant, Mary will be especially busy this tax season. That makes a night in with Bill and a Michelin-approved meal an especially welcome respite, she admitted. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School 6th grade teacher Ted Scherman and his wife Lisa will be celebrating their 25th anniversary in the summer this year. For this story, the Schermans made time to discuss their relationship, even though it was on Lisa’s birthday and Super Bowl Sunday, a big event for the couple and their three sons. This Valentine’s Day they will be remembering how they met, a tale that had both of them laughing and glowing visibly even through the phone. The sparks literally flew when Ted and Lisa first met. It was at a bonfire at The Lair of the Bear Campground outside the town of Strawberry in 1990. Both Ted and Lisa were on the UC Berkeley tennis team at the time and the bonfire was for all the staff and counselors at a summer tennis camp. Strawberry is in Tuolumne County off State Route 108.. Ted had already graduated but was at the camp because his coach was there and so were his former teammates. As luck would have it, he would meet the teammate of his life there as well. Asked what she remembered about meeting Ted, Lisa laughed heartily and said, “It was really funny, I saw him and this thought came into my head ‘I’m going to marry that person.’ I was all of 19.” After the bonfire Ted invited Lisa to play pool at the Berry, a bar in the town with a population of possibly 10 people. They had a nice time, Lisa recalled. The new tandem won their pool matches, a power couple from the start. The next day Lisa was dismayed that she could not find Ted. “I was asking around, where did that cute guy go?” she said. He was gone. In the middle of the night Ted had to leave the camp, and head back to Berkeley due to a painful attack of shingles which prevented him from sleeping. Three months later, Lisa got separated from her friends walking to Memorial Stadium for The Big Game, Cal vs. Stanford. “I kept looking for my friends, wondering where they were, thinking they were probably scattered. Before I could really look for them, I heard someone saying, ‘Lisa!’ I looked across and it was Ted. We ended up watching the Big Game together.” After the game, Lisa’s “hippie-friend Barb” whom Lisa had met once, invited Ted, Lisa and Ted’s friends to a party at the Lothlorien, the vegetarian co-op in the hills. The caveat is that it was a bit of a risqué and unusual event, a food party where you can’t feed yourself and there are no utensils. Ted’s friends all said no, and Lisa said she had a split-second thought that “If Ted says no, he might be too conservative for me.” Ted jumped at the opportunity, saying “I’ll go!” So off they went to Lothlorien, a beautiful 100-year-old building known for its arts and activism since the 70s. Inside, there was a giant chocolate fountain, and lots of fruit for fondue. Lisa recalled the events fondly. ”It was so fun, and this song by Spandau Ballet that goes “I Know This Much is True” was playing and we danced to that. We had our first kiss there, and the rest is history.” Valentine’s Day is more like Valentine’s Week in the Scherman BETWEEN GILMAN & BUCHANAN ST. 1081 Eastshore Hwy. Berkeley
articles.title: Ted and Lisa Scherman’s secret to relationship success: laughter

For this story, the Schermans made time to discuss their relationship, even though it was on Lisa’s birthday and Super Bowl Sunday, a big event for the couple and their three sons. This Valentine’s Day they will be remembering how they met, a tale that had both of them laughing and glowing visibly even through the phone. The sparks literally flew when Ted and Lisa first met. It was at a bonfire at The Lair of the Bear Campground outside the town of Strawberry in 1990. Both Ted and Lisa were on the UC Berkeley tennis team at the time and the bonfire was for all the staff and counselors at a summer tennis camp. Strawberry is in Tuolumne County off State Route 108.. Ted had already graduated but was at the camp because his coach was there and so were his former teammates. As luck would have it, he would meet the teammate of his life there as well. Asked what she remembered about meeting Ted, Lisa laughed heartily and said, “It was really funny, I saw him and this thought came into my head ‘I’m going to marry that person.’ I was all of 19.” After the bonfire Ted invited Lisa to play pool at the Berry, a bar in the town with a population of possibly 10 people. They had a nice time, Lisa recalled. The new tandem won their pool matches, a power couple from the start. The next day Lisa was dismayed that she could not find Ted. “I was asking around, where did that cute guy go?” she said. He was gone. In the middle of the night Ted had to leave the camp, and head back to Berkeley due to a painful attack of shingles which prevented him from sleeping. Three months later, Lisa got separated from her friends walking to Memorial Stadium for The Big Game, Cal vs. Stanford. “I kept looking for my friends, wondering where they were, thinking they were probably scattered. articles.text: Piedmont couple Hari Titan and his wife Roopal Desai are looking forward to spending their Valentine’s Day rather constructively this year – with a home improvement project. As a gift to his wife of 18 years, Hari said he plans on replacing the windows in their home after receiving the green light from the city to begin the project. Roopal said she is looking forward to the improvement, since both she and Hari have been observing strict stay-at-home orders since March one year ago. The couple does not plan on having a traditional Valentine’s Day dinner out at a restaurant due to the current health crisis. “We do the usual every year – dinner out or a movie,” Roopal said. “This year is definitely different – a more practical Valentine’s Day.” Hari added that the gift of manual labor trumps the traditional chocolates and flowers. “What says ‘I love you’ more than diamonds?” Hari said with a chuckle. Hari, a Ph.D Data Scientist, has been working remotely throughout the pandemic, but Desai, a physician with a specialty in Internal Medicine, will be working an overnight shift at Kaiser Permanente Medical Center. She added that she was immersed in her work when she first met Hari in Alameda 20 years ago in 2001. “I was completing my residency [at Alameda County Medical Center] and was working such long shifts,” she recalled. “My friends and family would ask me, how will you meet someone when you’re always so busy working?” The couple met through mutual friends, which was convenient for Roopal, who quipped, “I didn’t have to go out and look for someone.” Roopal and Hari were married in 2003 and moved with their son and daughter to Piedmont in 2008. Since then, the couple has been active throughout the community and the schools. Now, the couple has focused on a very pertinent goal – getting kids back for in-class instruction safely. They hope their decision to spend this special holiday at home will set an example for others to do the same. articles.text: Ashara Ekundayo San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora will host a forum on Tuesday, February 16 with guest curator Ashara Ekundayo in conversation with Yoruba Richen and Maori Holmes. The Zoom event will begin at 4 p.m. The forum, entitled “Blatant,” is a “live zine” series authored by Ekundayo that focuses on experiences of Black female artists. It is presented in conjunction with Ekundayo’s “Artist As First Responder” platform, a monthly discussion that highlights artists whose creative practices help heal communities. Richen is an award-winning documentary filmmaker. Her film, How it Feels To Be Free, premiered on PBS’s American Masters in January last month. Recent films include, The New York Times Presents: The Killing of Breonna Taylor, which premiered on FX and Hulu, and The Sit In: Harry Belafonte Hosts the Tonight Show, which was broadcast on MSNBC and is streaming on Peacock. Holmes is a curator, filmmaker and writer. She founded BlackStar in 2012 and serves as its Artistic Director and CEO. She has organized programs in film at a myriad of organizations including Anthology Film Archives, Los Angeles’ Museum of Contemporary Art, The Underground Museum, and the Whitney Museum of American Art. To reserve a place on Zoom, click on: https://www.moadsf.org/ event/blatant-a-forum-on-art-joyand-rage-8/?instance_id=15913.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera is making archived performances available for free through its “Opera is On” streaming series. Next up is Mozart’s romantic comedy, Cosi Fan Tuttee, which will stream on February 13 and 14 in time for Valentine’s Day. The short title, Così fan tutte, in Italian literally means, “so do they all,” and is usually translated into English as “women are like that.” It is considered Mozart’s most divisive and controversial work. In fact, Così fan tutte wasn’t popular with Mozart’s contemporaries who dismissed it as clumsy and miserable; as such, it was largely ignored. Despite being premiered in 1790, Così fan tutte didn’t become popular until the middle of the 20th century, though still dogged with accusations of misogyny. The opera follows best friends, Guglielmo and Ferrando, who are engaged to two sisters who are utterly faithful. Their relationships are put to the test in a tale of adultery and deception, wrapped in Mozart’s comedic style. Former San Francisco Opera Music Director Nicola Luisotti conducted the star-studded ensemble, which includes Ellie Dehn, Susannah Biller, and Marco Vinco. As the two men at the heart of the ruse, Francesco Demuro sings with “ardency and tonal brilliance,” while Philippe Sly delivers a Company debut “at once robust and lyrical,” the San Francisco Chronicle hailed. Visit https://sfopera.com/ opera-is-on /streaming/ for streaming instructions. The opera will be available only on February 13 and 14.

articles.text: Filoli House and Garden in Woodside has conducted a haiku contest to complement its “Winters at Filoli” calendar of events. The finalists will be announced via Zoom on Valentine’s Day, Sunday, February 14. Special guest judge and San Mateo County Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto will read the winning poem online on Sunday. In addition to her laureate status, Cassinetto is the publisher of Paloma Press, an independent press that publishes poetry and prose. Widely anthologized, she is also the author of the poetry collections, Traje de Boda and The Pink House of Purple Yam Preserves & Other Poems, as well as three chapbooks through Moria Books’ acclaimed Locofo series. Her work has appeared in the Asahi Shimbun, The Banyan Review, Moss Trill, The Nonconformist Magazine, the San Francisco Chronicle, and Vox Populi. Winter at Filoli is a time of Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto quiet and reflection in the garden, and individuals in the haiku competition were asked to submit a poem inspired by Filoli’s winter garden. The winner will receive a Household Plus Membership at Filoli, in addition to a gift basket of Filoli goodies. To see poems of the finalists, see https://filoli.org/haiku/ on February 10, The winner will be shown online on February 14 at 12 p.m. when Cassinetto will read the winning poem.

articles.text: Olga and Sergey Rakitchekov will perform a concert on Valentine’s Day, Sunday, February 14, as part of the Main Stage concerts of Gold Coast Chamber Player of Lafayette. Lafayette’s Gold Coast Chamber Players continues its virtual concerts with a series of six new programs. The next performance in their Main Stage Concerts is “Russian Valentine,” a love story of two musicians with a program for viola and harp. The concert features Olga and Sergey Rakitchekov, and will begin on Valentine’s Day, Sunday, February 14 at 4 p.m. Audience members will get a glimpse of the couple’s home life and their history beginning in 1968 at the Moscow Conservatory of Music. Their concert features the music of Debussy, Smirinov, Reger, and Bridge. articles.text: Ever dream of being a composer? Like so many things these days, everything is a formula. Since I am the musical gourmet, I offer you recipes for musical compositions. Choose your musical style and follow the recipe. The “One Chord” style. The easiest composition style is to master one chord on the piano. That’s it. One chord. When I was a kid there was a comedic song entitled “Johnny one note”. That was funny. But today, that is being a real composer. One chord on the piano. Who would have dreamt that the preposterous of the past would become today’s reality? I was in Rocky‘s Market on Leimert Blvd. about a week ago and they were playing some background music. While I was shopping I noticed that the pianist played the same chord over and over again...and no other cord. My internal metronome told me that the tempo was about 200 beats per minute. I figured the song lasted about 5 min. Simple arithmetic tells us that equals 1000 times playing the same note. Some of the people in the store seemed to enjoy this “music.” One chord played at least 1000 times! Sic gloria mundi. Country music I have always been a fan of classic country music and consider Hank Williams to be a treasure. His music spoke to the heart and soul of the human condition. I think this type of universality speaks to every human being. Some of Hank’s songs send chills up and down my spine. His poetry was pretty good, also. But that was the past. Today’s country music is all formula. Poetry? Forget about it. For lyrics, read from the newspaper and make sure your voice cracks on the first note of every sentence. The musical formula reads as follows: A guitar plays a four-chord introduction followed by heartbreak. Then dirt roads followed by something about Jesus. Remember to include something about America and finally some brief twangy chords to conclude. Be sure to have the recording engineer turn down the volume at the end. Cash imitating Elvis Presley. That’s a lesson in succinct and hilarious musical criticism. Blues, Pop, Rock Next is a recipe for success in blues composing: play a few chords on the guitar as an introduction then devote the bulk of the song to complaining and lamenting, and finish off with a few guitar chords. Keep repeating the same chords but have the recording engineer turn the volume down at the end. Maybe pop is your thing. This is a little bit more complicated. Pop music is often in five parts. Start out with a brief guitar introduction, and follow that with a simple “original” tune. Be sure to include a strange key change in the middle and then have the guy who’s twiddling the knobs create a fade out to nothing. Classic rock is also in about five sections. Be sure to include a brief verbal introduction telling everybody your resin Detra. (Sic!) while playing some chords on the guitar. Now turn up the volume on your electric guitar and twang away for a while and then either have some girls dancing or talk about girls, and then your drummer plays a solo and conclude with telling everybody how great the experience was. Have the recording engineer turn the volume down at the end. Despite what you hear on the news, there are some pretty funny things out there. And a lot of that passes for music. So… get your music manuscript paper ready. You have the recipe to be a (successful) composer. Laughing songs There are other inspirations. Among them are a great variety of laughing songs where somebody starts to play a song. Someone in the band plays a wrong note and that starts a cascade of laughing. “Spike Jones laughing record” comes to mind first. Then there were a number of “party records.” Some of the greatest Classical artists would record themselves doing absolutely ridiculous things. One of the best is available on YouTube. Look up “Jascha Heifetz Audition” and also the Johnny Cash imitation of Elvis Presley. Both are classics. Another is by Jo Stafford, who with her conductor/arranger husband Paul Weston, made a recording under the name Jonathan and Darlene Edwards. They lampooned popular music by singing familiar songs deliberately off-key and out of rhythm. You will be very happy that you explored this aspect of music. It is a complete delight, filled with insight, originality and plenty of side-splitting humor. In memoriam On a personal note, I note the passing of George Shultz at the ripe old age of 100. I got to know George through his sonin-law. What an honor. He had the insight of genius, because he knew what would happen even before it happened. He also had the wisdom to know what to do in every event. This is a gift given to very few. All of us hope that some of that insight will be passed on to future generations.
articles.title: Reality is hilarious

articles.text: Acronyms – helpful time saving devices? Or the tools of cult members to empower and keep secret their shorthand wisdom? Acronyms, the shortening of phrases of words into a series of first letters, can unnecessarily throw veils of confusion between a lay person and the adept. They started off as items of convenience, but soon acronyms have been wielded to cordon off wisdom from the seeker. Oh, how I hate acronyms. There are so many. Somehow, they throw off my pneumatic devices of memory. Should it be so difficult to receive full names, titles and explanations? Too many acronyms can easily bore and convolute. With sorrow I lament the fact that the use of acronyms in many industries is not only commonplace put a prerequisite for rudimentary discussion. Take the automotive industry, few wizards of wordcraft dwell in that realm. More commonly in the grease monkey world the virtues of the literate are shunned and laughed at. Car mechanics are ballerinas amongst machines, but butchers of the tongue. Nearly every automotive term has an associated acronym. RPMs, MPGs, SUVs, AWD, and PSI are common ones that have weaseled their way into the colloquial speech of all. Dig into an automotive textbook however, and the acronyms outnumber all adjectives, proper nouns, and adverbs combined. Acronyms are made for no reason at all, but the obvious observation that each word happens to begin with a letter. Are acronyms like WOT (wide open throttle), DTR (daytime running lights), and CVT (continuously variable transmission) really necessary? Using the actual words usually explains things correctly thoroughly. Daytime running lights? Hmm, those must be the little yellow lights that are on all the time. The complicated Continuously Variable Transmission is actually just like it sounds. Instead of having five gears of a fixed size, the continuously variable transmission uses a type of adjustable pulley mechanism always changing the tension of a transmission belt. The worst set of acronyms are three sets of letters that invite confusion and misunderstanding: KOER-Key On Engine Running KOEC-Key On Engine Cranking KOEO-Key On Engine Off Notice the shortening of three-letter words into one letter. A two-letter word shortened to one letter, “ON” to “O.” Really? Laziness or expedience? The worst part is that sometimes an O stands for On and sometimes for Off. And make sure not to confuse KOEO with Key Off Engine Off (that’s not a thing). But there is no Key On Engine On, that is covered with KOER (Key on Engine Running). This set of letters is supposed to be shorthand for the position your key is in while in the ignition. When you look at your car, those positions are labeled something else: LOCK, ACCESSORIES, START and RUN. My mustard-stained mustache boss eventually fired me from my lube tech position at the ole shop, but in a way I am glad. It’s like being banished from the cult before they start handing out the Kool-Aid. There are a few exceptions that prove the rule, however. For example, “SCUBA” sounds so cool that people don’t even realize it’s an acronym for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus. That’s a mouthful, so using an acronym makes sense. A personal favorite, which I suppose is the rare homophone acronym, is JEEP. It resulted from military men being fed up with the lazily named GP (general purpose) vehicles, so they sounded out the G and the P together. It must be acknowledged that acronyms can be used unjustly. Sometimes they are convenient, but they also can be used to privatize knowledge, or merely as an excuse to feign creativity. I will leave this discussion by quoting epic fantasy author Patrick Rothfuss from his first novel The Name of the Wind (2007): “What color is that boy’s shirt?” “Blue.” “What do you mean by blue? Describe it.” I struggled for a moment and failed. “So blue is a name?” “It is a word. Words are pale shadows of forgotten names. As names have power, words have power. Words can light fires in the minds of men. Words can produce tears from the hardest hearts. There are seven words that will make a person love you. There are ten words that will break a strong man’s will. But a word is nothing but a painting of a fire. A name is the fire itself.” My head was swimming by this point. “I still don’t understand.” He laid a hand on my shoulder. “Using words to talk of words is like using a pencil to draw a picture of itself, on itself. Impossible. Confusing. Frustrating.”
articles.title: HUMOR O.H.I.H.A. (Oh How I Hate Acronyms)

A two-letter word shortened to one letter, “ON” to “O.” Really? Laziness or expedience? The worst part is that sometimes an O stands for On and sometimes for Off. And make sure not to confuse KOEO with Key Off Engine Off (that’s not a thing). But there is no Key On Engine On, that is covered with KOER (Key on Engine Running). This set of letters is supposed to be shorthand for the position your key is in while in the ignition. When you look at your car, those positions are labeled something else: LOCK, ACCESSORIES, START and RUN. My mustard-stained mustache boss eventually fired me from my lube tech position at the ole shop, but in a way I am glad. It’s like being banished from the cult before they start handing out the Kool-Aid. There are a few exceptions that prove the rule, however. For example, “SCUBA” sounds so cool that people don’t even realize it’s an acronym for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus. That’s a mouthful, so using an acronym makes sense. A personal favorite, which I suppose is the rare homophone acronym, is JEEP. It resulted from military men being fed up with the lazily named GP (general purpose) vehicles, so they sounded out the G and the P together. It must be acknowledged that acronyms can be used unjustly. Sometimes they are convenient, but they also can be used to privatize knowledge, or merely as an excuse to feign creativity. I will leave this discussion by quoting epic fantasy author Patrick Rothfuss from his first novel The Name of the Wind (2007): “What color is that boy’s shirt?” “Blue.” “What do you mean by blue? Describe it.” I struggled for a moment and failed. “So blue is a name?” “It is a word. Words are pale shadows of forgotten names. As names have power, words have power. Words can light fires in the minds of men. Words can produce tears from the hardest hearts. There are seven words that will make a person love you. There are ten words that will break a strong man’s will. But a word is nothing but a painting of a fire. A name is the fire itself.” My head was swimming by this point. “I still don’t understand.” He laid a hand on my shoulder. “Using words to talk of words is like using a pencil to draw a picture of itself, on itself. Impossible. Confusing. Frustrating.” ADVERTISE IN THE POST

articles.text: Ralston Louie, a Piedmont High School graduate in 2010, died on January 31 after a swimming accident. He was 28. In the Winter of 2019-20, Ralston and his father travelled together back to the village in China to take photos and film video for Ralston’s master’s thesis. Since his return, he had been working hard to finish what promised to be a breakthrough project. From his family, Ralston always had a love for China. He studied in Beijing during college, and a fellowship allowed him to continue studying Chinese and live in Taiwan after graduating from Williams. He traveled throughout different cities and provinces of China as a young adult, eager to learn more about the history of his cultural heritage and gain a greater understanding of himself. Much of his studies, creative work and projects revolved around his roots and what it meant to be Asian American. Ralston always aspired to learn more. He carried a camera with him wherever he went, as a way to capture every moment he could. He was a true storyteller, someone who engaged with the world and found every opportunity to create work to share with others. As an avid athlete, Ralston continued to find new forms of physical activity throughout his life. Growing up he played soccer, basketball, golf, football, ran track, and was an expert skier. He continued to play soccer at the collegiate level. After college, Ralston discovered a love for surfing, swimming, trail running, and biking. He enjoyed days where he could simply be outside, swim in the ocean and catch waves for hours. He was a true water man. During his time at USC he joined the Triathlon Team, learning to train for future races. Ralston is survived by his parents, Robin Wu and Reagan Louie, and his sister, Ryan Louie. Donations in Ralston’s memory may be made to the “Vivian and Stanley Wu and Ralston Louie Fund” of the Asian Pacific Fund at 465 California Street, Suite 809, San Francisco, CA 94104 or secure.qgiv.com/for/apfund. articles.text: The important quality of life characteristic of a place that planners call “walkability” now seems to be recognized and highly valued everywhere. It is considered an amenity to any neighborhood, and property values are positively affected by a good walkability rating. Simply stated, walkability is how userfriendly an area is for pedestrians; how easy, convenient and safe it is to walk from one place to the next. I am fond of this relatively recent term because as readers of this column know, I value and enjoy walking for many reasons. While in much of today’s world we have designed and built our communities to accommodate the car at the expense of pedestrians, travel on foot will always be the most basic and socially valuable form of getting around. Walking is a community enhancer. When people are on foot, the pace is slow enough to really observe immediate surroundings and the opportunity to meet and talk to other people exists, something that is pretty much impossible when we are isolated from one another in our cars. Like many planning concepts, walkability is strongly linked to other issues and considerations, and chief among them is density. If things are too spread out (low density), walking any distance doesn’t make sense much of the time. But if destinations are close enough (higher density), walking to school, church, stores or the park are feasible – and they’re healthy and fun. The walkability rating of Piedmont, like any city, varies based on the conditions in any local area. Unfortunately, published walkability scores have become inflated due to the economic value of high ratings. The only way to truly know is to judge for yourself. This map of the city shows an approximation of some walking times to the center. Variables include the steepness of the walk in addition to distance. It suggests that while we certainly can’t conveniently walk everywhere we need to go, many of us can easily walk to some of our destinations. Camino de Santiago sketches: The most remarkable example of a place with true walkability this writer has seen is in northern Spain, along the famous Camino de Santiago. People make treks of hundreds of miles solely on foot along routes that support and cater in every way to….walking! I think that much of the rest of the world can learn from this place.

The walkability rating of Piedmont, like any city, varies based on the conditions in any local area. Unfortunately, published walkability scores have become inflated due to the economic value of high ratings. The only way to truly know is to judge for yourself. This map of the city shows an approximation of some walking times to the center. Variables include the steepness of the walk in addition to distance. It suggests that while we certainly can’t conveniently walk everywhere we need to go, many of us can easily walk to some of our destinations. There are many different reasons to walk and many of the benefits overlap. It’s possible to cover all the examples shown above in a single walk. But maybe the most important requirement for true walkability is a positive response to the question, “Is this a nice place to walk?” Piedmont certainly is. Some may be surprised to learn that Piedmont is a relatively dense city: twice that of Walnut Creek or Hayward, and five times greater than Orinda. Here, the higher density makes the city automatically more walkable. Terrain however, is also a factor. The steeper hilly areas in town have the opposite effect, making walking more strenuous and less convenient. Proximity of destinations is also important in determining how convenient it is to walk. Piedmont’s central core area is full of parks and civic uses but has very limited commercial and business uses. If for example you want something from a pharmacy, it is necessary to go out of town. But like “open space” that we discussed in the last column, because of proximity, we are the beneficiaries of various walkable retail districts in Oakland just outside Piedmont. If we are able to walk more, we mitigate many obvious problems endemic to our culture, including traffic jams and auto pollution. Just a small reduction in auto trips replaced by walking can make a significant difference. But perhaps most important of all, is the health benefit of walking. Researchers tell us that everything from cardiovascular strength, to healthy blood pressure, to energy boosts are improved by even a minimum amount of walking on a regular basis. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its Zoom book discussion on February 1, with 15 readers on the call to discuss their two February selections. Led by Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long, the group had a lively discussion about Olive Kitteridge, the first Olive novel by writer Elizabeth Strout, and Olive, Again, the second book. Participating in the discussion were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Bella Almanzan, Sally Arney, Albert Chen, Pat McSwain, Karin Fetherston, and Dick Carter. Olive Kitteridge was published in 2008 and received critical acclaim. It was awarded the Pulitzer Prize and was made into an HBO four-part miniseries. The title character, Olive Kitteridge, is a retired schoolteacher, who lives in the fictional town of Crosby, Maine. The novel is structured into 13 chapters that are much like a set of short stories. In Crosby everyone knows everyone else’s business, and that can include murder, pedophilia, suicide, armed robbery, arson, and also true love and deep sadness. As the townspeople struggle with their problems, Olive develops a deeper understanding of herself and her life, sometimes painfully, but always honestly. This is the journey of a complex, blunt, opinionated, cantankerous woman as she grows older and interacts with her family and the members of her small town. Olive says exactly what she is thinking, and often seems to act with little regard for others’ feelings. Her targets can include her two husbands and her son, who can’t tolerate her, yet still seem to love her. Olive’s husbands accept Olive as she is with her off-putting behavior and personality, but they also love her. Strout followed up in 2019 on the success of Olive Kitteridge with a sequel, Olive, Again. Similar to the first novel, Olive, Again takes the form of 13 short story chapters that are interrelated and follow Olive from age 70 into her eighties. At the end of the book and her life, readers see Olive showing greater empathy and having a realization that, while she often tried to help others, she knows that she could have done better. The books were well received by most members of the group. Readers appreciated Strout’s detailed, descriptive, and beautiful writing; and enjoyed the stories of the different people within the novels. Strout is a masterful writer. She presents the feelings of the books’ different characters, and especially Olive, in ways that the readers found very real. Olive’s aging process and growth also provided opportunities for introspection, with some readers saying that they hope they don’t turn out like Olive. articles.text: Emmy Fearn is guest speaker for zoom meeting on Feb, 22 Seniors who want to maintain their health and stay out of the emergency room will want to participate in a presentation scheduled for Monday, February 22 at 3 p.m. on Zoom. Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, a discussion by Emmy Fearn will describe the causes of dehydration, its danger and symptoms, how very quickly dehydration can occur, and most importantly, how to prevent it. All Piedmont seniors are invited. To receive the Zoom link to join the meeting, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. Fearn, a resident in nearby Crocker Highlands, became interested in the impact of dehydration when her otherwise healthy mother collapsed and was hospitalized, after becoming dehydrated in less than a day. Fearn has provided talks on dehydration to seniors at Piedmont Gardens, at Kaiser Hospital, and to the Piedmont Seniors. Fearn has a doctorate in Special Education and has taught at San Francisco State and CSU East Bay. She currently supervises new Special Education teachers at Mills College. Led by Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long, the group had a lively discussion about Olive Kitteridge, the first Olive novel by writer Elizabeth Strout, and Olive, Again, the second book. Participating in the discussion were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Bella Almanzan, Sally Arney, Albert Chen, Pat McSwain, Karin Fetherston, and Dick Carter. Olive Kitteridge was published in 2008 and received critical acclaim. It was awarded the Pulitzer Prize and was made into an HBO four-part miniseries. The title character, Olive Kitteridge, is a retired schoolteacher, who lives in the fictional town of Crosby, Maine. The novel is structured into 13 chapters that are much like a set of short stories. In Crosby everyone knows everyone else’s business, and that can include murder, pedophilia, suicide, armed robbery, arson, and also true love and deep sadness. As the townspeople struggle with their problems, Olive develops a deeper understanding of herself and her life, sometimes painfully, but always honestly. This is the journey of a complex, blunt, opinionated, cantankerous woman as she grows older and interacts with her family and the members of her small town. Olive says exactly what she is thinking, and often seems to act with little regard for others’ feelings. Her targets can include her two husbands and her son, who can’t tolerate her, yet still seem to love her. Olive’s husbands accept Olive as she is with her off-putting behavior and personality, but they also love her. Strout followed up in 2019 on the success of Olive Kitteridge with a sequel, Olive, Again. Similar to the first novel, Olive, Again takes the form of 13 short story chapters that are interrelated and follow Olive from age 70 into her eighties. At the end of the book and her life, readers see Olive showing greater empathy and having a realization that, while she often tried to help others, she knows that she could have done better. The books were well received by most members of the group. Readers appreciated Strout’s detailed, descriptive, and beautiful writing; and enjoyed the stories of the different people within the novels. Strout is a masterful writer. She presents the feelings of the books’ different characters, and especially Olive, in ways that the readers found very real. Olive’s aging process and growth also provided opportunities for introspection, with some readers saying that they hope they don’t turn out like Olive. However, not all the readers were lovers of the books. While appreciating Strout’s writing, some readers simply did not like the character of Olive. It’s possible to turn away from fear by gaining a clearer view of God as Love itself, which can have a tangible, healing effect in your life and in the world. At 5 p.m. on Thursday, February 18, tune in to a free, live Zoom lecture entitled, “Spiritual Discovery in a Time of Upheaval” by Tom McElroy, a Christian Science practitioner and teacher. The discussion is sponsored by First Church of Christ, Scientist in Oakland. “Prayer is about spiritual discovery. It’s about understanding more of what God is and learning to see our lives and the world through the lens of God’s all-good nature. It’s about stripping away surface-level appearances in order to discern what actually is,” explained McElroy. “Spiritual discovery reveals what is substantial, lasting, and powerful, and this leads to healing. What’s the outcome? Progress. Transformation. Wholeness – for anyone.” The link to attend the online talk is on the Church’s website, www.ChristianScienceOakland.org. articles.text: An early 20th century look at Piedmont Park When Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898, only the Clubhouse, the rustic teahouse, the mineral springs and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and wandering paths were there to attract visitors to the park. Havens continued to add more attractions to draw visitors to Piedmont Park and to the city itself. Many visitors enjoyed the weather and views and decided to build their homes here. Frank Havens and his Realty Syndicate was there to sell them a home site. In 1904 he built “The Maze.” Gardeners planted a large circular hedge maze in the natural bowl where Witter Field stands today. This privet maze challenged all who entered to reach the bright red pagoda at the center. Ladders strategically placed throughout the Maze allowed those feeling hopelessly lost to climb a ladder to the top of the hedge and get their bearings. And true to the nature and design of mazes, the Maze in Piedmont was a double challenge; the return trip out of the Maze was just as challenging as that to the center. lower entrance to Piedmont Park. Havens developed a lane from Grand Avenue to the Maze and on to the park paths. He lined it with palm trees, some of which still survive on what is now Palm Drive. The Maze from 1904 is now the location of the high school’s Witter Field. One year after the 1906 earthquake and fire in San Francisco, Havens added more attractions to Piedmont Park. Many refugees from San Francisco fled to the East Bay, and Havens wanted to draw them to Piedmont and sell them property for building homes. In keeping with the Victorian interest in the exotic, Havens added a Japanese Tea House. Built as a replica of the late-fifteenth century Silver Pavilion in Kyoto, Japan, the teahouse opened in 1907 where today’s Japanese Tea House stands. (The current tea house was moved to Piedmont Park in 1976 from an estate where Piedmont Middle School now stands.) A Japanese gate led to a Japanese-style garden with ponds and a moon bridge. Stickwork fences, pillars and benches complemented these Japanese grounds. Also in 1907, Havens built his Piedmont Art Gallery on the site of today’s tennis courts in the park. The spacious art gallery had a large skylight and was built to display Havens’ collection of 375 pieces of art by English, French, Russian, American and other painters. Two additional gallery wings extended beyond the main gallery. Eleven countries in all were represented by this collection. The centerpieces of Havens’ collection were 162 large Russian masterpieces that were exhibited at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. After the exposition, the paintings were stored in Canada. In order to avoid paying customs This rustic teahouse was built near today’s bus shelter. fees on the paintings, they were unscrupulously appraised far below their value. Havens and his agent then snatched them up at a fraction of their worth. Havens was particularly fond of California impressionists, and his collection also included work by William Keith, Charles Rollo Peters, Gordon Couts, Thomas Hill, Xavier Martinez and others. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Couts lived and painted in Piedmont at this time. Havens’ art collection was said to be one of the finest collections in the country. Havens charged admission to the Art Gallery, and artist Richard Partington, Havens’ sister-in-law Carrie Sterling and son Seyd Havens served successively as curators of the gallery. In 1916, Havens had plans to develop the park into residential home sites. He sent his paintings to San Francisco where they were auctioned off. Some paintings went to private collectors, some to the new Oakland Art Museum, and many went to the de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
